title: Microbiology: Introduction and General Bacteriology
subject: Microbiology
description: 80 practice MCQs in two parts of 40 questions each.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A laboratory team studies microbial metabolism, transmission, pathogenesis, identification, treatment, and prevention. Which description best captures the scope of their discipline?

options.A: The study of visible organisms only
options.B: The study of microorganisms and their biological and medical relationships
options.C: The study of infectious diseases without studying their agents
options.D: The study of human immunity alone

questions.explanation: Medical microbiology examines medically important microorganisms and includes their structure, growth, metabolism, genetics, transmission, pathogenesis, identification, treatment, and prevention.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A researcher uses a simple microscope to observe living bacteria, protozoa, and yeasts, but cannot observe viruses. Which historical figure best matches this work?
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek used high-quality simple lenses to observe living microorganisms, including bacteria, protozoa, and yeasts; viruses were beyond the resolving capability of his microscopes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A student claims that maggots arise directly from rotting meat. Which experimental observation most directly challenges this claim?

options.A: Maggots grow faster at higher temperatures
options.B: Maggots appear on gauze covering meat but not on the meat when flies are excluded
options.C: Meat decomposes when kept in darkness
options.D: Meat contains nutrients for microbial growth

questions.explanation: Redi showed that when flies could not reach the meat, maggots did not develop on the meat; larvae were associated with fly access and egg deposition.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Why did critics initially object to Spallanzani’s sealed, boiled-broth experiment?

options.A: They argued that broth contained no nutrients
options.B: They argued that boiling created microorganisms
options.C: They argued that air was necessary for life and had been excluded
options.D: They argued that the container was too large

questions.explanation: Critics argued that the absence of growth resulted from lack of air rather than prevention of contamination, leaving the question unresolved until Pasteur’s design.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which feature made Pasteur’s swan-neck flask especially effective against the criticism of Spallanzani’s experiment?

options.A: It prevented air from entering the flask
options.B: It allowed air to enter while trapping contaminating particles in the curved neck

questions.explanation: The curved neck permitted free diffusion of air while particles carrying microorganisms were trapped in the bend, addressing the argument that air itself was required.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A swan-neck flask remains clear while upright but becomes cloudy after broth is tipped into the neck and returned to the flask. What is the strongest inference?

options.A: Air spontaneously creates microorganisms when broth is moved
options.B: Broth cannot support bacterial growth unless tilted
options.C: Microorganisms in the environment contaminate the broth; they are not spontaneously generated by air
options.D: Boiling broth permanently removes all nutrients

questions.explanation: Tilting allows broth to contact trapped contaminants in the neck, after which growth occurs; this supports contamination from pre-existing microorganisms rather than spontaneous generation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A surgeon introduces chemical treatment of wounds using phenol to reduce infections during surgery. Which historical figure is most closely associated with this development?
questions.explanation: Lister applied germ-theory concepts to antiseptic surgery and popularized chemical inhibition of infection, including the use of phenol on surgical wounds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which statement most accurately represents the germ theory of disease?

options.A: All illnesses are caused by bacteria
options.B: Many diseases are caused by microorganisms
options.C: Microorganisms cause disease only after death
options.D: Disease is caused by invisible spirits rather than biological agents

questions.explanation: Germ theory proposes that microorganisms cause many diseases; it does not claim that every disease is infectious or that all pathogens are bacteria.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which sequence most closely follows the logic of Koch’s postulates?

options.A: Treat disease, identify symptoms, vaccinate, culture blood
options.B: Observe an organism in disease, isolate and culture it, introduce it into a healthy susceptible host, reproduce disease, then reisolate it
options.C: Observe an organism in a healthy host, destroy it, and infer causation
options.D: Culture any organism and assume it causes the disease

questions.explanation: The classic sequence links a candidate organism to disease by observation, isolation/culture, reproduction of disease in a susceptible host, and reisolation of the same organism.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A suspected pathogen is repeatedly associated with disease, but it cannot be grown on artificial media. Which limitation of Koch’s postulates does this illustrate?

options.B: Some microorganisms are difficult or impossible to cultivate in the laboratory
options.C: Microorganisms cannot be isolated from diseased hosts
options.D: Disease can only be studied in plants

questions.explanation: The classical postulates rely on isolation and laboratory cultivation, which is not feasible for certain organisms, such as those noted in the course material.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A microorganism is found in many healthy people without symptoms. Which conclusion best reflects a limitation of the classical postulates?

options.A: The organism must be harmless in every host
options.B: The organism cannot ever cause disease
options.C: Presence of an organism alone may not establish that it causes disease in every carrier
options.D: The organism must be a fungus

questions.explanation: Asymptomatic carriage means a pathogen may be present without disease, so the simple rule that it is found only in diseased individuals does not always hold.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which situation creates an ethical barrier to testing Koch’s postulates directly in humans?

options.A: The organism has a distinctive shape
options.B: A healthy human volunteer would need to be deliberately infected with a dangerous pathogen
options.C: The organism grows rapidly on agar
options.D: The organism can be stained by Gram stain

questions.explanation: Deliberately infecting a person with a pathogen can be ethically unacceptable, especially when humans are the only suitable host.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which combination best explains why microorganisms are widely distributed in air, water, soil, and living bodies?

options.A: Large size, slow reproduction, and narrow metabolism
options.B: Small size, diverse forms, rapid reproduction, adaptability, easy transmission, and diverse metabolism
options.C: Dependence on a single nutrient and one environmental condition

questions.explanation: The material identifies small size, forms such as spores or cysts, adaptability, rapid reproduction, transmission, and metabolic diversity as factors supporting widespread distribution.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A biotechnology laboratory uses yeast and bacteria to investigate basic biochemical pathways. Which advantage most directly supports their use as model organisms?

options.B: They reproduce rapidly and have relatively simple genetics and biochemistry
options.C: They are all harmless to humans

questions.explanation: Rapid reproduction and comparatively simple genetic and biochemical systems make bacteria and yeast useful for studying fundamental life processes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A factory uses microorganisms to break down toxic waste materials. Which application is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to degrade or remove toxic waste materials and is an ecological application of microbiology.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Dough rises after yeast is added and supplied with sugar and oxygen. Which process described in the course material is most directly associated with this use?

options.D: Binary fission of yeast cells alone

questions.explanation: The material describes aerobic respiration by yeast using sugar in dough, producing carbon dioxide that helps the bread rise.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A brewer limits oxygen availability so yeast converts sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Which process is occurring?
questions.explanation: In the absence of oxygen, yeast converts sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide; the material identifies this as fermentation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A nurse breaks one essential link in the chain of infection by performing hand hygiene before patient contact. What is the most accurate general interpretation?

options.B: Transmission can be interrupted even if the infectious agent remains in its reservoir
options.C: The pathogen is necessarily eradicated from the environment
options.D: The susceptible host becomes permanently immune

questions.explanation: The chain of infection requires connected events; interrupting transmission can prevent spread without eliminating the agent from every reservoir.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A patient develops an infection caused by microorganisms normally present on their own skin after a procedure breaches the barrier. How is the source best classified?
questions.explanation: An endogenous infection originates from the person’s own normal flora when conditions allow those organisms to cause disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A healthcare worker carries bacteria from one patient to another on unclean hands. The source of the organisms for the second patient is best described as:
questions.explanation: The organisms are introduced from outside the second patient, making this an exogenous source; contaminated healthcare-worker hands can carry them between patients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which option is the best definition of a microbial reservoir?

options.A: The route by which an organism enters a host
options.B: A place where a microorganism lives, grows, and reproduces
options.C: The symptom caused by microbial toxins
options.D: A laboratory method for staining bacteria

questions.explanation: Reservoirs are places in which microorganisms grow and reproduce; examples include humans, animals, food, water, soil, and healthcare equipment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A person with an intestinal infection contaminates the surrounding environment while defecating. Which portal of exit is involved?
questions.explanation: Feces and vomitus are routes by which microorganisms can leave a reservoir through the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A susceptible host acquires an organism through sexual intercourse with an infected person. Under the classification used in the material, this is:
questions.explanation: Sexual intercourse is listed as direct transmission because the agent passes through immediate contact between the source and susceptible host.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A contaminated towel transfers a microorganism from one person to another. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: A towel is an inanimate intermediary, or fomite, and therefore represents indirect transmission.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A mosquito carries an infectious agent between hosts. Which route is involved?
questions.explanation: A vector is a living intermediary such as a mosquito, flea, or tick that carries an infectious agent between hosts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which example most clearly represents vehicle-borne transmission rather than vector-borne transmission?

options.B: A tick carries an infectious agent
options.D: An infected person touches another person

questions.explanation: Water is an inanimate vehicle that carries the infectious agent; mosquitoes and ticks are living vectors.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Bacteria travel upward along an indwelling urinary catheter and enter the bladder. Which portal of entry is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The material describes bacteria ascending a urinary catheter into the bladder as entry through the genitourinary tract.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A classification system groups organisms by convenient observable traits even when those traits do not necessarily indicate evolutionary relatedness. Which system is this?
questions.explanation: Phenetic classification groups organisms by observable or convenient characteristics; phylogenetic classification aims to reflect genetic similarity and evolutionary relationships.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Two microorganisms are grouped together because molecular evidence indicates close genetic and evolutionary relatedness, despite some visible differences. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Phylogenetic classification is intended to reflect genetic similarity and evolutionary relatedness rather than relying only on observable traits.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A microorganism has no membrane-bound nucleus, usually circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and no mitochondria. Which cellular organization does it have?
questions.explanation: These are core features of prokaryotes: a nucleoid rather than a membrane-bound nucleus, usually circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, and absence of membrane-bound organelles.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which feature most strongly distinguishes a eukaryotic cell from a typical bacterial cell?

options.C: A membrane-bound nucleus containing linear chromosomes

questions.explanation: Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus with linear chromosomes, whereas bacterial DNA is typically circular and located in the nucleoid.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A student attempts to place a virus into one of the three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, or Eukarya. What is the best response?

options.A: Viruses belong to Eukarya because they contain nucleic acid
options.B: Viruses belong to Archaea because they are ancient
options.C: Viruses are acellular and do not fit within the three-domain system
options.D: Viruses are a fourth cellular domain in this system

questions.explanation: The material describes viruses as acellular and outside the three-domain system, which classifies cellular life as Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: An organism contains chlorophyll, has a cell wall, and performs photosynthesis. Which group best fits the description used in the material?
questions.explanation: Algae are described as chlorophyll-containing, photosynthetic eukaryotes with cell walls.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A colorless eukaryotic microorganism ingests organic particles and lacks a cell wall. Which group is most consistent with these characteristics?
questions.explanation: Protozoa are described as colorless organisms that ingest other organisms or organic particles and lack a cell wall.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A laboratory uses the reaction of a bacterial isolate with antibodies specific to its antigens, producing visible clumping. Which identification method is being used?
questions.explanation: Specific antibodies bind their corresponding bacterial antigens and can produce agglutination, making this a serological method.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium is exposed to a bacteriophage known to infect a specific bacterial type; a clear plaque forms where bacterial cells are destroyed. Which method is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Phage typing exploits the specificity of bacteriophages for certain bacteria; susceptible cells are destroyed, creating plaques in the bacterial lawn.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A laboratory compares ribosomal RNA sequences to determine evolutionary relationships among isolates. Which type of evidence is being used?
questions.explanation: Ribosomal RNA sequencing is a molecular approach used to classify microorganisms by genetic relatedness.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A Gram stain is performed on a clinical specimen. Which set of findings should be included in the report according to the material?

options.A: Patient age, drug dose, and prognosis
options.B: Number of bacteria, Gram reaction, morphology, and intra-/extracellular location
options.C: Only the color of the counterstain
options.D: Only whether the culture is positive

questions.explanation: The material specifies bacterial quantity, Gram reaction, morphology, and whether organisms are intracellular or extracellular as reporting elements.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which example shows why the classical postulates cannot be applied mechanically to every disease?

options.A: A pure culture is obtained from a pathogen
options.B: A disease has a single identifiable bacterial cause
options.C: A disease results from mixed infection involving more than one microorganism
options.D: The organism can be observed microscopically

questions.explanation: Mixed infections challenge a framework designed to link one specific microbe to one specific disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial cell has surface appendages, a cell envelope, and a cytoplasmic region containing DNA and ribosomes. Which structure-function pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Flagella are protein appendages that provide motility; pili are mainly involved in attachment and conjugation, while ribosomes synthesize proteins.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A donor bacterium transfers genetic material to a recipient through direct cell-to-cell contact. Which structure most directly facilitates the contact described?
questions.explanation: Conjugation pili connect donor and recipient bacteria and facilitate one-way transfer of DNA from donor to recipient.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium has a single flagellum at one pole. Which arrangement is described?
questions.explanation: Monotrichous means one flagellum at one end; lophotrichous means a tuft at one end, amphitrichous means at both ends, and peritrichous means distributed around the cell.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial isolate has flagella at both ends of the cell. Which arrangement should be recorded?
questions.explanation: Amphitrichous describes flagella at both ends of a bacterial cell.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Compared with a slime layer, a capsule is best described as:
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx may occur as a capsule, which is organized and tightly attached, or as a loosely organized slime layer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial mutant loses its capsule but retains the ability to grow in nutrient broth. Which outcome is most consistent with the capsule's functions?

options.A: The organism necessarily cannot synthesize proteins
options.B: It may become less able to resist host defenses or adhere, despite continued growth

questions.explanation: The capsule is not essential for growth under all conditions but contributes to adhesion, protection from white-cell killing, biofilm formation, and virulence.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Bacteria in a dental plaque persist despite host defenses and antimicrobial exposure. Which feature best explains this persistence in the material?

options.A: The biofilm provides protection from antibiotics and host defenses
options.B: The bacteria have no cell wall
options.C: The bacteria are unable to attach to surfaces
options.D: The bacteria are all obligate anaerobes

questions.explanation: The material identifies biofilm as a protective community associated with surfaces, such as dental plaque, that can reduce susceptibility to antibiotics and host defenses.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Why are bacterial cell-wall synthesis pathways important targets for antimicrobial drugs?

options.A: Cell walls are identical to human mitochondrial membranes
options.B: Cell walls contain distinctive components and are crucial for bacterial growth and division
options.C: Cell walls are present in every virus
options.D: Cell walls are the only site of bacterial DNA

questions.explanation: Bacterial cell walls contain unique structures such as peptidoglycan and are essential for viability, making their synthesis useful for selective antimicrobial targeting.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which description best explains the mechanical rigidity of the bacterial cell wall?

options.B: Linear polysaccharide chains cross-linked by peptides
options.D: A membrane made only of phospholipids

questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan consists of linear amino-sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides, providing strength and rigidity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which combination is most characteristic of a Gram-positive bacterial cell wall?

options.A: Thin peptidoglycan, outer membrane, and LPS
options.B: Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids and no outer membrane
options.C: No peptidoglycan and no cell membrane
options.D: Waxy mycolic acids as the defining feature of all Gram-positive bacteria

questions.explanation: Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan and commonly contain teichoic and lipoteichoic acids; they lack the Gram-negative outer membrane containing LPS.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial envelope contains an outer membrane, thin peptidoglycan, and a periplasmic space with beta-lactamase. Which group is most likely?
questions.explanation: The material describes Gram-negative bacteria as having thin peptidoglycan, an outer membrane, and a periplasmic space that can contain hydrolytic enzymes including beta-lactamase.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A component of the outer membrane triggers a powerful inflammatory response and is associated with fever and shock. Which molecule is responsible, and which part is toxic?
questions.explanation: LPS is also called endotoxin; its Lipid A component is the toxic part and can stimulate cytokine release associated with fever and shock.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which LPS component is especially useful for distinguishing antigenic variants of bacteria?
questions.explanation: The O antigen contributes antigenic variation and is useful in bacterial typing, whereas Lipid A is the toxic component.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial isolate resists drying and many chemicals and stains poorly with routine Gram stain. Its wall contains abundant waxy lipid. Which component best explains these properties?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterial cell walls contain waxy mycolic acids, which contribute to acid-fastness, resistance to desiccation and some antimicrobial effects, and pathogenicity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which organism is specifically identified in the material as lacking a conventional bacterial cell wall?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma species are listed among bacteria lacking a cell wall, along with L-forms, spheroplasts, and protoplasts.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A drug selectively interferes with bacterial protein synthesis by acting on the bacterial ribosome. Which ribosomal size is typical of bacteria?
questions.explanation: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, composed of 50S and 30S subunits; eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are typically 80S.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial isolate rapidly acquires a resistance determinant carried on a small circular DNA molecule that replicates independently of the chromosome. What is the most likely genetic element?
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small circular double-stranded DNA molecules that may carry antibiotic-resistance genes, toxins, or enzymes and can be transferred between cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A laboratory assigns a standardized two-part scientific name to an isolate. Which rule is correct?

options.A: Both genus and species begin with capital letters
options.B: The genus is capitalized, the specific epithet is lowercase, and the full name is italicized or underlined
options.C: Only the species epithet is written in italics
options.D: The name must describe the patient's symptoms

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature uses a genus name followed by a specific epithet; the genus begins with a capital letter, the epithet is lowercase, and the full name is italicized or underlined.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: Which method is genotypic rather than phenotypic?
questions.explanation: Guanine-cytosine ratio, nucleic-acid sequence, plasmid, ribotyping, and chromosomal DNA analyses are genotypic methods.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: After Gram staining, a bacterium appears pink. Which cell-envelope feature best explains this result?

options.A: A thick peptidoglycan layer retains crystal violet
options.B: A thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane permit decolorization before counterstaining
options.C: A complete absence of a plasma membrane
options.D: A capsule converts crystal violet into safranin

questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria are decolorized by alcohol because of their envelope structure and then take up the pink/red counterstain.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A sputum smear is treated with carbol-fuchsin, acid-alcohol, and methylene blue. Acid-fast bacilli remain pink against a contrasting background. What explains this retention?

options.A: Their peptidoglycan is always thicker than Gram-positive bacteria
options.B: Their lipid-rich, mycolic-acid-containing wall retains the primary dye despite acid-alcohol

questions.explanation: The lipid-rich mycobacterial wall containing mycolic acid gives acid-fastness, allowing organisms to retain carbol-fuchsin after acid-alcohol decolorization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A technician observes 6 acid-fast bacilli across 100 high-power fields. Using the scale presented in the course material, how should this be graded?
questions.explanation: The scale defines scanty as 1–9 AFB per 100 high-power fields; 10–99 per 100 fields is 1+.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A Gram-positive coccus forms grape-like irregular clusters. Which arrangement is most consistent with this observation?
questions.explanation: Staphylococci are cocci arranged in irregular grape-like clusters, while streptococci typically form chains and diplococci occur in pairs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A rod-shaped bacterium remains attached at angles, producing a Chinese-letter appearance. Which organism is the example associated with this morphology?
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is described as bacilli attached at various angles resembling Chinese letters.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A small, slightly curved Gram-negative rod is observed. Which bacterial shape category best fits?
questions.explanation: Vibrios are small, slightly curved rods and are described as Gram-negative; Vibrio cholerae is a representative example.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: An organism is flexible, coiled, motile, and difficult to stain by the Gram method. Which group is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Spirochaetes are flexible coiled motile organisms with rapid body movements and are often not easily stained by Gram methods.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium obtains carbon from inorganic carbon dioxide rather than depending on organic compounds. Which nutritional category best describes it?
questions.explanation: Autotrophs use inorganic compounds such as CO2 as a carbon source, whereas heterotrophs depend on organic compounds.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial species grows best at 60°C. According to the temperature ranges given, which group best fits?
questions.explanation: The listed thermophile range is approximately 45–75°C; hyperthermophiles grow at still higher temperatures.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium can grow using aerobic respiration when oxygen is present but can also grow by fermentation or anaerobic respiration when it is absent. Which category fits?
questions.explanation: Facultative anaerobes can maintain life using aerobic respiration when possible or fermentation/anaerobic respiration when oxygen is unavailable.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium requires oxygen concentrations lower than atmospheric levels, approximately 5–10%, and has limited ability to detoxify reactive oxygen products. Which category is indicated?
questions.explanation: Microaerophiles require reduced oxygen concentrations and have limited ability to detoxify hydrogen peroxide and superoxide radicals.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A culture shows rapid population increase, peak metabolic activity, young delicate cells, and high sensitivity to antibiotics and UV light. Which phase is this?
questions.explanation: The log phase is characterized by rapid, exponential division, high metabolic activity, and relative susceptibility to antibiotics and UV light.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: In a bacterial culture, the number of cells formed equals the number dying, nutrients are depleted, and waste accumulates. Which phase is represented?
questions.explanation: The stationary phase is an equilibrium between new cells and dying cells and is associated with nutrient depletion and waste accumulation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A culture becomes Gram-variable and cells die faster than they are produced because nutrients are exhausted and toxic wastes accumulate. Which phase is occurring?
questions.explanation: In the death phase, viable cells decline because death exceeds replication; the material also notes Gram-variable staining during this phase.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterial population increases from 1,000 to 8,000 cells under ideal conditions. How many generations have occurred?
questions.explanation: Each generation doubles the population: 1,000 → 2,000 → 4,000 → 8,000. This is three doublings, so n = 3.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A specimen is thought to contain very small numbers of a pathogen. The laboratory first uses a medium and conditions intended to increase that organism's numbers before isolation. Which medium strategy is being used?
questions.explanation: Enrichment media promote multiplication of a desired organism when its initial number in a specimen is low, facilitating later isolation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A laboratory wants a medium that suppresses Gram-positive bacteria while permitting Gram-negative bacteria to grow. Which medium from the material best fits?
questions.explanation: EMB contains methylene blue, which inhibits Gram-positive bacteria and allows growth of Gram-negative organisms; it can also differentiate fermentation patterns.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A medium permits growth of selected bacteria and also distinguishes organisms by visible changes related to lactose fermentation. Which statement best describes its properties?

options.A: It is only enriched and cannot be selective
options.B: It can be both selective and differential
options.C: It is a stain rather than a culture medium
options.D: It is used only for viruses

questions.explanation: MacConkey and EMB are examples that select for Gram-negative organisms and differentiate based on carbohydrate fermentation reactions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacterium acquires free DNA fragments from its surroundings and incorporates genetic information from them. Which mechanism is involved?
questions.explanation: Transformation is uptake of isolated DNA from the surrounding medium; conjugation requires direct cell contact, while transduction is phage-mediated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A donor bacterium carrying a fertility plasmid transfers DNA directly to an F− recipient through cell contact. Which mechanism is occurring?
questions.explanation: Conjugation transfers DNA by direct contact between bacterial cells; the material describes transfer from an F+ donor to an F− recipient.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A bacteriophage mediates transfer of bacterial genes from one bacterium to another. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Transduction is gene transfer mediated by a bacteriophage, distinguishing it from free-DNA uptake in transformation and direct contact in conjugation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A pharmaceutical company studies microorganisms that can produce antibiotics and vaccines while also monitoring contamination of its products. Which branch of microbiology most directly covers this work?
questions.explanation: Pharmaceutical microbiology focuses on microorganisms involved in producing antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, vitamins, and other pharmaceutical products, as well as microbial contamination and spoilage.
